name: Chromolithograph poster
region: Paris, then all of Europe and the United States
summary: A large poster drawn in crayon and brush on stones, one stone for each colour. Jules Chéret printed his first colour posters in Paris in 1866 with a few strong inks; Mucha, Toulouse-Lautrec and the Beggarstaffs made the street a gallery.

philosophy.core_thesis: A few bright inks, drawn by the artist on stone, can make a sheet on a wall as bright and as alive as a painting.
design_principles: Use 3–5 inks: a dark key for the drawing, a red, a yellow and a blue, with mixed tones where they overprint.
Draw the key with a lithographic crayon, so the tone has the grain of the stone.
Make one large figure, often a woman in motion, fill most of the sheet.
Put the name of the product or the show in hand-drawn letters at the top or the bottom, in the same inks.
Use spatter (crachis) and crayon grain for the half tones; keep flat colour for large areas.
Let the colours shift a little from the key; the eye accepts a small misregister.
anti_patterns: Typeset text in one plain face
Many small images in a grid

process.matrix: Bavarian limestone, one stone for each ink, drawn with a greasy crayon and tusche.
process.press: A steam-powered flatbed lithographic press, with sheets up to 2.5 m long printed in parts.
process.image_making: The artist draws the key; a chromiste separates the colours by hand on the other stones from a tracing.
process.edition: Thousands of posters for a campaign, plus small editions on good paper for collectors.

inks.strategy: A dark key and three or four bright inks; the half tones come from the crayon and from overprints.

screening.rule: Make the tone with the grain of the crayon on the stone and with spatter; there is no screen.

registration.rule: Each stone registers to pins; a shift of 0.5–1 mm is common and shows as a light rim.

substrate.stock: A thin machine-made poster paper; collectors' copies on heavier wove.
substrate.finish: Uncoated, smooth, with a slight tooth.

surface.impression: No bite: the ink lies flat on the sheet.
surface.sheen: Matt, with a soft sheen in the dark inks.
surface.texture: A grain of crayon and spatter in the half tones, with flat areas of strong colour.

emotion.target_response: Joy and spectacle: the viewer feels the pleasure of the city at night, a café or a show.

avoid_when: The message needs a photograph or a lot of small text.
The brand must look sober or technical.

modifiers.how: Add a halo and a frame of whiplash lines and flowers round the figure, in the manner of Mucha.
Drop the grain for flat, opaque colours put on through stencils, with a thin key line.

sources.title: Ruth E. Iskin, The Poster: Art, Advertising, Design, and Collecting, 1860s–1900s (Dartmouth, 2014)
